title: Genesis 31:22–55
context: On the third day Laban hears that Jacob has fled and pursues him seven days into Gilead, but God warns Laban in a dream to say nothing to Jacob, good or bad. The camps meet; Laban charges trickery and stolen gods; Jacob pleads fear that the daughters would be taken by force. Rachel hides the teraphim in a camel's saddle while Laban searches the tents. Jacob's anger then recounts twenty years of labor, and he names the God who saw his affliction. They raise a heap—Galeed and Mizpah—calling God to watch between them; Jacob swears by the Fear of Isaac, they sacrifice and eat, and in the morning Laban blesses his grandchildren and daughters and turns home.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: How earlier teachers on both sides handled Laban’s pursuit, the dream-warning, and the Mizpah covenant, quoted directly.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Speak not, either good or bad—That is, say nothing against his going on with his journey, for the thing proceedeth from the Lord. The same Hebraism we have, Gen 24:50. The safety of good men is very much owing to the hold God has of the consciences of bad men, and the access he has to them.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 31:24)

reformed.quote: The Lord gave to his servant the interval of a three-days' journey, so that having passed the Euphrates, he might enter the boundaries of the promised land. By afterward permitting Jacob to be intercepted in the midst of his journey, God intended to tender his own interposition the more illustrious. It seemed desirable that Jacob's course should not be interrupted, and that he should not be filled with alarm by the hostile approach of his father-in-law; but when Laban, like a savage wild beast, breathing nothing but slaughter, is suddenly restrained by the Lord, this was far more likely to confirm the faith of the holy man, and therefore far more useful to him.

verses.text: Laban was told on the third day that Jacob had fled.
verses.arminianNotes: Laban learns of the flight on the third day—ordinary news that still leaves him a responsible pursuer. Delay is mercy, not an excuse to hunt without conscience.
verses.reformedNotes: Three days pass before the report arrives. Providence has already given Jacob a head start on the road of promise before Laban ever saddles for Gilead.

verses.text: He took his relatives with him, and pursued him seven days’ journey. He overtook him in the mountain of Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes: Laban freely gathers kinsmen and pursues seven days into Gilead; the threat is human agency, not fate. Grace will restrain harm, but the chase itself is a chosen act.
verses.reformedNotes: Seven days of pursuit cannot outrun the God who will meet Laban in the night. The close follow into Gilead is permitted only so that the confrontation unfolds under a word already prepared.

verses.text: God came to Laban the Syrian in a dream of the night, and said to him, “Be careful that you don’t speak to Jacob either good or bad.”
verses.arminianNotes: God comes and warns: say nothing to Jacob, good or bad. The night word is a command Laban can and must heed, grace restraining harm by a sincere warning.
verses.reformedNotes: The dream is effectual restraint. God comes to the Aramean, speaks, and will keep Jacob from Laban's mouth and hand before the camps even meet.
verses.keyContrast: Both honor the dream as God's word. Arminians typically emphasize an earnest warning Laban can heed; Reformed readers press effectual restraint that preserves the promised seed.

verses.text: Laban caught up with Jacob. Now Jacob had pitched his tent in the mountain, and Laban with his relatives encamped in the mountain of Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes: Two camps pitch in Gilead by travel and choice. The meeting is now a moral confrontation, not a raid already finished in blood.
verses.reformedNotes: Over-taking is allowed, but only after the night word. Providence sets the tents facing each other under a restraint Laban did not invent.

verses.text: Laban said to Jacob, “What have you done, that you have deceived me, and carried away my daughters like captives of the sword?
verses.arminianNotes: Laban names trickery and daughters driven like captives of the sword—actual family harm. Deceit remains culpable even when flight was needed.
verses.reformedNotes: The charge is loud, yet God has already limited what Laban can do. The conflict now unfolds under a spoken leash, not under Laban's full power.

verses.text: Why did you flee secretly, and deceive me, and didn’t tell me, that I might have sent you away with mirth and with songs, with tambourine and with harp;
verses.arminianNotes: Laban claims he would have sent them with music. Whether sincere or self-serving, secret flight still cost a farewell, and stealth is a choice.
verses.reformedNotes: The protest of tambourine and lyre cannot rewrite twenty years. God, not Laban's feast, is the true sender of Jacob toward the land of promise.

verses.text: and didn’t allow me to kiss my sons and my daughters? Now you have done foolishly.
verses.arminianNotes: Withholding a farewell kiss is a deep grief. Jacob's fear does not erase the family cost of leaving in stealth, and Laban's charge of folly must be heard.
verses.reformedNotes: Wounded affection sits beside the dream that already forbade harm. Folly is named; the God who spoke in the night still holds the scene.

verses.text: It is in the power of my hand to hurt you, but the God of your father spoke to me last night, saying, ‘Be careful that you don’t speak to Jacob either good or bad.’
verses.arminianNotes: Laban admits both power to harm and a divine warning. Grace restrains a man who could still choose violence; the night word is an earnest command, not theater.
verses.reformedNotes: "It is in the power of my hand" meets "But the God of your father." Effectual speech from the dream now governs the confrontation and keeps Jacob for the promise.

verses.text: Now, you want to be gone, because you greatly longed for your father’s house, but why have you stolen my gods?”
verses.arminianNotes: Homesickness is granted; stealing household gods is a crime Laban may justly name. Theft remains theft even when Laban's own piety is mixed.
verses.reformedNotes: The teraphim charge will expose Rachel, yet the God who spoke in the night is no household idol. Providence will keep Jacob even through a theft he does not yet know.

verses.text: Jacob answered Laban, “Because I was afraid, for I said, ‘Lest you should take your daughters from me by force.’
verses.arminianNotes: Jacob answers with honest fear: he thought Laban would take the daughters by force. Moral agency includes fear, flight, and the need to tell the truth about motive.
verses.reformedNotes: The fear is deeply felt, and so is the God who has already blocked Laban. Jacob's motive does not carry the story; the night word does.

verses.text: Anyone you find your gods with shall not live. Before our relatives, discern what is yours with me, and take it.” For Jacob didn’t know that Rachel had stolen them.
verses.arminianNotes: Jacob's rash vow is speech with deadly stakes; ignorance of Rachel's theft does not make the oath wise. He invites a public search he cannot control.
verses.reformedNotes: The narrator's aside is mercy: Jacob does not know. Providence will keep the search from blood even under a foolish curse.

verses.text: Laban went into Jacob’s tent, into Leah’s tent, and into the tent of the two female servants; but he didn’t find them. He went out of Leah’s tent, and entered into Rachel’s tent.
verses.arminianNotes: Laban searches tent by tent; theft is treated as an offense requiring evidence. The hunt is thorough, and still a moral act, not mere theater.
verses.reformedNotes: The search proceeds tent by tent, yet the gods remain hidden. God can frustrate a hunt without Jacob lifting a hand.

verses.text: Now Rachel had taken the teraphim, put them in the camel’s saddle, and sat on them. Laban felt around all the tent, but didn’t find them.
verses.arminianNotes: Rachel's ruse is moral agency—theft plus concealment—not a cute trick beyond judgment. Sitting on the teraphim is a chosen deceit.
verses.reformedNotes: The saddle hides what Laban cannot find. Providence uses even a daughter's deceit to keep the confrontation from the blood Jacob's vow invited.

verses.text: She said to her father, “Don’t let my lord be angry that I can’t rise up before you; for I’m having my period.” He searched, but didn’t find the teraphim.
verses.arminianNotes: Rachel's excuse is another layer of deceit toward her father. Grace that hides the idols does not baptize the lie; she remains a responsible actor.
verses.reformedNotes: Laban searches and does not find. The Fear of Isaac is preserving a household even while teraphim sit under a saddle and a false word.

verses.text: Jacob was angry, and argued with Laban. Jacob answered Laban, “What is my trespass? What is my sin, that you have hotly pursued me?
verses.arminianNotes: Anger and a demand for named sin are fair once the search fails. Jacob may seek justice without denying his own earlier stealth.
verses.reformedNotes: The hot pursuit now looks empty. God has already rebuked Laban; Jacob's protest rides a deliverance already given.

verses.text: Now that you have felt around in all my stuff, what have you found of all your household stuff? Set it here before my relatives and your relatives, that they may judge between us two.
verses.arminianNotes: Public evidence before kinsmen is a sincere appeal to communal justice. Empty hands should end the charge, and neighbors are called to decide.
verses.reformedNotes: Nothing of Laban's is found because God kept the search from succeeding. The court of kinsmen sits inside providence.

verses.text: “These twenty years I have been with you. Your ewes and your female goats have not cast their young, and I haven’t eaten the rams of your flocks.
verses.arminianNotes: Twenty years of faithful labor is stewardship Jacob may justly claim. Grace does not erase honest work or the right to name it.
verses.reformedNotes: Flocks kept and rams uneaten are the fruit of a God who was with Jacob. The record is true; the Giver stands behind the years.

verses.text: That which was torn of animals, I didn’t bring to you. I bore its loss. Of my hand you required it, whether stolen by day or stolen by night.
verses.arminianNotes: Jacob bore losses Laban required—injustice in the wage. Moral agency includes both the shepherd's integrity and the master's greed.
verses.reformedNotes: What Laban required, God saw. The night rebuke answers years of extracted loss, not only one secret flight.

verses.text: This was my situation: in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep fled from my eyes.
verses.arminianNotes: Heat, cold, and sleeplessness are not pious exaggeration. Hardship freely endured can still be named before a hard kinsman.
verses.reformedNotes: Heat, cold, and sleeplessness were the path by which God kept His man. Suffering served the promise, not Laban's kindness.

verses.text: These twenty years I have been in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters, and six years for your flock, and you have changed my wages ten times.
verses.arminianNotes: Changed wages ten times name Laban's culpable cheating. Jacob's fourteen years and six were service that should have been honored.
verses.reformedNotes: Fourteen and six are counted years under a God who did not permit the cheat to empty Jacob. The ledger is human; the preservation is divine.

verses.text: Unless the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, surely now you would have sent me away empty. God has seen my affliction and the labor of my hands, and rebuked you last night.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jacob credits the God of his father with seeing affliction and rebuking Laban. Grace that takes a side still leaves Laban a warned moral agent who heard a serious word.
verses.reformedNotes: Without the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, Jacob would be empty-handed. Effectual help preserved the promised man, and last night's rebuke was God's own.
verses.keyContrast: Both let Jacob give God the credit. Arminians emphasize God seeing affliction and issuing a rebuke Laban must heed; Reformed interpreters underline that the Fear of Isaac effectually kept Jacob for the promise.

verses.text: Laban answered Jacob, “The daughters are my daughters, the children are my children, the flocks are my flocks, and all that you see is mine! What can I do today to these my daughters, or to their children whom they have borne?
verses.arminianNotes: Laban still claims everything, then admits he cannot harm his own daughters and their children—an if late, moral check. Family love can restrain what pride would seize.
verses.reformedNotes: Possession-talk meets the limit God already set. What Laban calls mine cannot stop the return God commanded or the rebuke already spoken.

verses.text: Now come, let’s make a covenant, you and I. Let it be for a witness between me and you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The offer of covenant is a sincere bid for peace that both men can actually keep. Vows are moral speech, not empty ceremony.
verses.reformedNotes: A witness between them will soon be named as God Himself. Human treaty sits under divine oversight that has already restrained harm.

verses.text: Jacob took a stone, and set it up for a pillar.
verses.arminianNotes: Jacob's pillar is a chosen sign of peace, not magic. He acts responsibly to mark the word they will swear.
verses.reformedNotes: A stone rises as God once met him at Bethel. The God of the promise now fences the border with a pillar Jacob is moved to set.

verses.text: Jacob said to his relatives, “Gather stones.” They took stones, and made a heap. They ate there by the heap.
verses.arminianNotes: Shared stones and a shared meal are peace-making. Eating by the heap seals intent, not mere ceremony, and kinsmen take part.
verses.reformedNotes: The heap and the meal are appointed means. God is turning pursuit into a table under His eye.

verses.text: Laban called it Jegar Sahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed.
verses.arminianNotes: Two tongues name one heap of witness. Language differs; the moral claim of a witnessed peace is the same and meant to bind.
verses.reformedNotes: Aramaic and Hebrew meet at a border God has drawn. The names will serve the oath He overhears.

verses.text: Laban said, “This heap is witness between me and you today.” Therefore it was named Galeed
verses.arminianNotes: Laban's naming makes the heap a public witness. Today's word is meant to bind tomorrow's conduct between two responsible men.
verses.reformedNotes: Today is God's timing after the night dream. The witness-heap stands because harm was already checked by the God who spoke.

verses.text: and Mizpah, for he said, “The LORD watch between me and you, when we are absent one from another.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD watch between me and you and me is a sincere invocation of God's moral gaze when distance removes human eyes. The prayer assumes God sees, and that both must live accordingly.
verses.reformedNotes: Mizpah is more than sentiment: the LORD Himself is the Watcher who keeps the promised line beyond Laban's reach, in sight or out of sight.
verses.keyContrast: Both take the watch as God's presence. Arminians typically hear a sincere prayer for moral accountability when apart; Calvinists hear God as the effectual Watcher who already preserved Jacob.

verses.text: If you afflict my daughters, or if you take wives in addition to my daughters, no man is with us; behold, God is witness between me and you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The terms are concrete: do not oppress, do not take other wives. God as witness makes the vow morally serious even when no human eye remains.
verses.reformedNotes: God is witness whether Laban is fully sincere or not. The daughters of the promise live under a Gaze Laban cannot dismiss.

verses.text: Laban said to Jacob, “See this heap, and see the pillar, which I have set between me and you.
verses.arminianNotes: Laban claims the setting of the markers. Taking responsibility for a boundary can still be a true step toward peace.
verses.reformedNotes: What Laban set sits inside what God already set in the dream. The border is human stone and divine will together.

verses.text: May this heap be a witness, and the pillar be a witness, that I will not pass over this heap to you, and that you will not pass over this heap and this pillar to me, for harm.
verses.arminianNotes: Mutual non-aggression is a covenant duty both can keep. The heap forbids harm as a chosen peace, not a mere monument.
verses.reformedNotes: The prohibition of harm echoes the night word. God has already forbidden Jacob's injury; the stones now publish what heaven spoke.

verses.text: The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us.” Then Jacob swore by the fear of his father, Isaac.
verses.arminianNotes: Laban invokes ancestral names in a shared formula; Jacob swears only by the Fear of Isaac. The distinction of worship is a responsible, public act.
verses.reformedNotes: Jacob will not merge the Fear of Isaac with Nahor's gods. The oath that binds him is the God who keeps the promise and has already judged the night.

verses.text: Jacob offered a sacrifice in the mountain, and called his relatives to eat bread. They ate bread, and stayed all night in the mountain.
verses.arminianNotes: Sacrifice and shared bread are sincere covenant seals. They spend the night as men at peace, not as raiders still choosing harm.
verses.reformedNotes: Worship and meal close the chase. The God who warned Laban now lets the camp sleep under a peace He has secured.

verses.text: Early in the morning, Laban rose up, and kissed his sons and his daughters, and blessed them. Laban departed and returned to his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Morning kisses and blessing are a farewell at last. Laban's return home is a chosen end to hostility, grace having restrained the harm he named.
verses.reformedNotes: Laban blesses and goes. Jacob is left on the road of promise because God restrained the pursuer, witnessed the heap, and sent him home.
